claim: A founding paradigm in virology is that the spatial unit of the viral replication cycle is an individual cell.
source: A founding paradigm in virology is that the spatial unit of the viral replication cycle is an individual cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field of virology.

claim: Multipartite viruses have a segmented genome where each segment is encapsidated separately.
source: Multipartite viruses have a segmented genome where each segment is encapsidated separately.
evidence: This is stated as a defining characteristic of multipartite viruses, representing established knowledge.

claim: In multipartite viruses, the viral genome is not recapitulated in a single virus particle but in the viral population.
source: In this situation the viral genome is not recapitulated in a single virus particle but in the viral population.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the separate encapsidation of segments.

claim: FBNSV genome segments rarely co-occur within individual cells.
source: By localizing and quantifying the genome segments of a nanovirus in host plant tissues we show that they rarely co-occur within individual cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental localization and quantification data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distinct FBNSV segments accumulate independently in different cells.
source: We further demonstrate that distinct segments accumulate independently in different cells and that the viral system is functional through complementation across cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental demonstration described in the manuscript.

claim: The FBNSV viral system is functional through complementation across cells.
source: We further demonstrate that distinct segments accumulate independently in different cells and that the viral system is functional through complementation across cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental demonstration described in the manuscript.

claim: The infection of nanoviruses can operate at a level above the individual cell level, defining a viral multicellular way of life.
source: Our observation deviates from the classical conceptual framework in virology and opens an alternative possibility (at least for nanoviruses) where the infection can operate at a level above the individual cell level, defining a viral multicellular way of life.
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Viruses introduce their genome into a susceptible cell and hijack diverse cell functions to complete their replication cycle.
source: Viruses introduce their genome into a susceptible cell and highjack diverse cell functions to complete their replication cycle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about viral replication.

claim: The universal view of the viral way of life has been applied to multipartite viruses since their discovery over half a century ago.
source: This universal view of the viral way of life has been applied to multipartite viruses since their discovery, over half a century ago (Brakke et al., 1951; Lister, 1966; van Kammen and van Griensven, 1970; Gokhale and Bald, 1987), despite the fact that such a conceptual framework fails to explain the evolution and even the functioning of these viral systems (Iranzo and Manrubia, 2012; Sicard et al., 2016; Lucía-Sanz and Manrubia, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: The cell-autonomous conceptual framework fails to explain the evolution and functioning of multipartite viral systems.
source: This universal view of the viral way of life has been applied to multipartite viruses since their discovery, over half a century ago (Brakke et al., 1951; Lister, 1966; van Kammen and van Griensven, 1970; Gokhale and Bald, 1987), despite the fact that such a conceptual framework fails to explain the evolution and even the functioning of these viral systems (Iranzo and Manrubia, 2012; Sicard et al., 2016; Lucía-Sanz and Manrubia, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Multipartite viruses have their genome composed of two to eight segments of DNA or RNA (single or double stranded), each encapsidated individually in a separate virus particle.
source: Depending on the viral species, multipartite viruses have their genome composed of two to eight segments of DNA or RNA (single or double stranded), each encapsidated individually in a separate virus particle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about multipartite viruses.

claim: Multipartite viruses have been reported to infect frequently plants and fungi where they represent at least 35–40% of the viral genera and families described.
source: They have been reported to infect frequently plants and fungi where they represent at least 35–40% of the viral genera and families described (Hull, 2014), rarely insects (Hu et al., 2016; Ladner et al., 2016), and only hypothetically vertebrates (Ladner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Multipartite viruses rarely infect insects.
source: They have been reported to infect frequently plants and fungi where they represent at least 35–40% of the viral genera and families described (Hull, 2014), rarely insects (Hu et al., 2016; Ladner et al., 2016), and only hypothetically vertebrates (Ladner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Multipartite viruses only hypothetically infect vertebrates.
source: They have been reported to infect frequently plants and fungi where they represent at least 35–40% of the viral genera and families described (Hull, 2014), rarely insects (Hu et al., 2016; Ladner et al., 2016), and only hypothetically vertebrates (Ladner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The benefits of the individual encapsidation of distinct segments are unclear and debated.
source: The benefits of the individual encapsidation of distinct segments are unclear and debated (Sicard et al., 2016; Lucía-Sanz and Manrubia, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The reduced probability to infect individual host cells with at least one copy of each segment is unanimously acknowledged as a major cost that increases with the number of segments composing the viral genome.
source: In contrast, the reduced probability to infect individual host cells with at least one copy of each segment is unanimously acknowledged as a major cost that increases with the number of segments composing the viral genome (Iranzo and Manrubia, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The cost of reduced probability to co-infect cells appears insurmountable, at least for viruses with more than three genome segments.
source: This cost appears insurmountable, at least for viruses with more than three genome segments, and sets the existence of such highly multipartite viruses as an enigma in general biology (Iranzo and Manrubia, 2012; Sicard et al., 2016; Lucía-Sanz and Manrubia, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The existence of highly multipartite viruses is set as an enigma in general biology.
source: This cost appears insurmountable, at least for viruses with more than three genome segments, and sets the existence of such highly multipartite viruses as an enigma in general biology (Iranzo and Manrubia, 2012; Sicard et al., 2016; Lucía-Sanz and Manrubia, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The empirical basis of the cost of multipartite viruses has never been questioned.
source: Nevertheless, its empirical basis has never been questioned.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the state of the field.

claim: FBNSV is a highly multipartite virus with eight genome segments.
source: Using a highly multipartite virus with eight genome segments, we here propose that the conceptual framework in Virology should be amended to account for such viral systems.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental model.

claim: The distinct segments of FBNSV do not need to be together in individual cells for the system to be functional.
source: Indeed, in our specific experimental model species, we demonstrate that the distinct segments do not need be together in individual cells for the system to be functional.
evidence: This is supported by experimental demonstration described in the manuscript.

claim: FBNSV segments accumulate independently in and complement across neighboring cells.
source: They accumulate independently in and complement across neighboring cells, defining a multicellular way of life.
evidence: This is supported by experimental demonstration described in the manuscript.

claim: The FBNSV genome is composed of eight circular ssDNA segments.
source: We used the highly multipartite faba bean necrotic stunt virus (FBNSV, genus Nanovirus, Family Nanoviridae), whose genome is composed of eight circular ssDNA segments (Figure 1A) (Grigoras et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Distinct FBNSV segments do not necessarily co-occur but are most often found in different cells.
source: In plants submitted to productive viral infection (see Materials and methods), the visualization of pairs of segments respectively labeled with green and red fluorochromes immediately revealed that distinct segments do not necessarily co-occur but are most often found in different cells (Figure 1B–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in figures.

claim: Seven out of the 28 possible pairs of FBNSV segments were tested for co-localization.
source: We tested 7 out of the 28 possible pairs of segments.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design.

claim: In all tested pairs of FBNSV segments, one segment was most often highly accumulated in the absence of the other in individual cells.
source: In all cases we observed a similar situation with one segment most often highly accumulated in the absence of the other in individual cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Cells containing all eight FBNSV segments are extremely rare.
source: Remarkably, this applied even to the pairs from the three segments encoding for the three basic functions of plant viruses: replication (segment R encoding M-Rep), encapsidation (segment S encoding CP) and intra-host movement (segment M encoding MP), suggesting that cells containing all eight segments are extremely rare.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that even functionally critical segment pairs do not co-localize.

claim: Segment R encodes M-Rep, which is responsible for replication.
source: replication (segment R encoding M-Rep)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FBNSV.

claim: Segment S encodes CP, which is responsible for encapsidation.
source: encapsidation (segment S encoding CP)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FBNSV.

claim: Segment M encodes MP, which is responsible for intra-host movement.
source: intra-host movement (segment M encoding MP)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FBNSV.

claim: When two distinct regions of the same segment R are labeled, all cells labeled by R1 are also labeled by R2.
source: As a positive control of this approach, we first produced two fluorescent probes, each specifically labeling a different region of the same segment R (probes R1 and R2). Figure 2 illustrates that all cells labeled by R1 are also labeled by R2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The average intensity of green over red fluorescence for cells labeled with two probes for the same segment R resulted in a highly significant linear relationship (correlation coefficient r = 0.90, p=1.98 10−23 in petiole N° 42).
source: Moreover, plotting the average intensity of green over red fluorescence for each of these cells resulted in a highly significant linear relationship (correlation coefficient r = 0.90, p=1.98 10−23 in the example of petiole N° 42 in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Four independent repeats of the control with two probes for segment R showed strong correlations.
source: Four independent repeats of this control similarly showed strong correlations (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: When two viral DNA sequences whose accumulation should be highly correlated are monitored, they co-localize and accumulate at highly correlated levels.
source: This result validates our approach by demonstrating that when we monitor two viral DNA sequences whose accumulation should be highly correlated, such as two regions of the same segment, we indeed find that they co-localize and accumulate at highly correlated levels.
evidence: This is supported by the control experiment with two probes for the same segment.

claim: Ten petioles from different plants infected independently were tested for the pair of segments R/S.
source: This approach was then extensively used for the pair of segments R/S because they encode the two key viral functions, replication and encapsidation. In total, we tested 10 petioles, each from a different plant infected independently.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental design.

claim: No significant correlation could be found for the accumulation of segments R and S in individual cells.
source: No significant correlation could be found (Figure 2C, Table 1), whether at early or late stages of infection (Table 1 and also see Figure 1—figure supplement 2), showing that the accumulation of the segment S in a cell is independent of that of the replication-encoding segment R.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: The accumulation of segment S in a cell is independent of that of the replication-encoding segment R.
source: No significant correlation could be found (Figure 2C, Table 1), whether at early or late stages of infection (Table 1 and also see Figure 1—figure supplement 2), showing that the accumulation of the segment S in a cell is independent of that of the replication-encoding segment R.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis showing no correlation.

claim: Five additional petioles from five independent plants were analyzed for pairs R/M and S/M, and no significant positive correlation was found.
source: We extended this analysis to five additional petioles from five independent plants, two for the pair R/M and three for the pair S/M, and again found no significant positive correlation; a result indicative of independent accumulation (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: If two segments independently enter and accumulate in individual cells, then their relative frequencies in infected tissues should be proportional to the ratio of the number of cells they respectively infect.
source: Within an infected petiole, if two segments independently enter and accumulate in individual cells, then their relative frequencies in infected tissues should be proportional to the ratio of the number of cells they respectively infect.
evidence: This is stated as a logical prediction based on independent accumulation.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the relative frequency of the segments in the tissues and the relative number of cells they respectively infect (n = 7, F = 12, R = 0.677, p-value=0.0122).
source: Figure 2D shows a significant correlation between the relative frequency of the segments in the tissues and the relative number of cells they respectively infect (n = 7, F = 12, R = 0.677, p-value=0.0122).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Two different technologies (FISH-confocal microscopy and quantitative real-time PCR) concur to demonstrate that the accumulation of distinct FBNSV segments in individual cells is independent.
source: Hence, two different technologies (FISH-confocal microscopy and quantitative real-time PCR) concur to demonstrate that the accumulation of distinct FBNSV segments in individual cells is independent.
evidence: This is supported by convergent results from two different experimental approaches.

claim: A viral function can be present and act in a cell where its encoding segment is not.
source: To make sense out of the above observation we assumed that a viral function can be present and act in a cell where its encoding segment is not, and thus that the viral system can be functional despite the independent dispersal of its distinct genes in distinct cells.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption to explain the observations.

claim: The viral system can be functional despite the independent dispersal of its distinct genes in distinct cells.
source: To make sense out of the above observation we assumed that a viral function can be present and act in a cell where its encoding segment is not, and thus that the viral system can be functional despite the independent dispersal of its distinct genes in distinct cells.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption to explain the observations.

claim: The segments detected in individual cells are the product of replication.
source: We first confirmed that the segments detected in individual cells are the product of replication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental confirmation described in the manuscript.

claim: Most individual cells (54% to 100%) contained only one detectable allele of segments S and N.
source: Three independent experiments were carried out for each of the segments S and N where two genetic markers have earlier been inserted (Gallet et al., 2017). They consistently revealed that most individual cells (54% to 100%) contained only one detectable allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), confirming that one to very few copies of the segment initially enter individual cells and thus that detection all over the nucleus can only result from replication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: One to very few copies of the segment initially enter individual cells.
source: They consistently revealed that most individual cells (54% to 100%) contained only one detectable allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), confirming that one to very few copies of the segment initially enter individual cells and thus that detection all over the nucleus can only result from replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most cells contain only one allele.

claim: Detection of segments all over the nucleus can only result from replication.
source: They consistently revealed that most individual cells (54% to 100%) contained only one detectable allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), confirming that one to very few copies of the segment initially enter individual cells and thus that detection all over the nucleus can only result from replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that few copies enter but are detected throughout the nucleus.

claim: Segment R was detectable in only approximately 40% of cells where segment S is detectable.
source: We then confronted the cells where the segment S is detectable (thus where it has replicated) to the detection of either segment R or its protein product M-Rep, by a combination of FISH and immunofluorescence-labeling (Figure 3A and B). While segment R was detectable in only a minority of these cells (approx. 40%), its protein product M-Rep was positively revealed in nearly 85% (Figure 3C), indicating that the expression product of R segment can move to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The protein product M-Rep was positively revealed in nearly 85% of cells where segment S is detectable.
source: While segment R was detectable in only a minority of these cells (approx. 40%), its protein product M-Rep was positively revealed in nearly 85% (Figure 3C), indicating that the expression product of R segment can move to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression product of R segment can move to neighboring cells.
source: While segment R was detectable in only a minority of these cells (approx. 40%), its protein product M-Rep was positively revealed in nearly 85% (Figure 3C), indicating that the expression product of R segment can move to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that M-Rep is present in more cells than segment R.

claim: Both mRNAs and proteins have a relatively rapid turnover within a cell, whereas the DNA viral sequences can be stored indefinitely into the cell nucleus.
source: Indeed, both mRNAs and proteins have a relatively rapid turnover within a cell, whereas the DNA viral sequences can be stored indefinitely into the cell nucleus either encapsidated or as stable minichromosomes (Gronenborn, 2004; Ramesh et al., 2017; Deuschle et al., 2016; Rodríguez-Negrete et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: For all cells where at least one FBNSV segment is detectable, the protein M-Rep is or has been present.
source: Thus, we assume that for all cells where at least one FBNSV segment is detectable the protein M-Rep is or has been present, but that this protein may have disappeared in some cases at the moment of the observation.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption based on protein turnover.

claim: A similar proportion of cells containing the segment R have M-Rep no longer detectable as cells containing segment S without detectable M-Rep.
source: Consistent with this assumption is the observation of a similar proportion of cells containing the segment R where its own expression product M-Rep is no longer detectable (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The protein M-Rep is detected, often with intense signal, in a large number of cells where segment R is absent.
source: It is important to note the detection of the M-Rep protein, often with intense signal (Figure 3A & B), in a large number of cells where segment R is absent (Supplementary file 1: Table S1, petioles 36–39).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A & B and Table S1.

claim: The protein M-Rep is not more associated to cells containing its own encoding segment R than to cells containing other segments.
source: Moreover, Figure 3C (orange middle and bleu-grey right boxplots) indicates that the protein M-Rep is not more associated to cells containing its own encoding segment R than to cells containing other segments.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Either the mRNA or the protein M-Rep itself can travel from the producing cells to other cells of the host.
source: Although they represent indirect evidence, these observations together further support our conclusion that either the mRNA or the protein M-Rep itself can travel from the producing cells (those where segment R accumulates) to other cells of the host, as further discussed below.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that M-Rep is present in cells without segment R.

claim: Key genome segments of the FBNSV accumulate in individual cells independently of the presence and accumulation of the others.
source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that key genome segments of the FBNSV accumulate in individual cells independently of the presence and accumulation of the others.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The different parts of the viral genome can complement across distinct neighboring cells and can only sustain the productive infection at a multicellular tissue level.
source: We thus propose that the different parts of the viral genome can complement across distinct neighboring cells and can only sustain the productive infection at a multicellular tissue level.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental results.

claim: Nanoviruses are restricted to vascular tissues and replicate in phloem companion and parenchyma cells.
source: As numerous other plant virus species (Hipper et al., 2013; Folimonova and Tilsner, 2018), nanoviruses are restricted to vascular tissues and replicate in phloem companion and parenchyma cells (Shirasawa-Seo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Each FBNSV genome segment entering and expressing within a cell can export its gene products as 'common goods' in neighboring cells and/or sieve elements.
source: A model compatible with our observations is that each genome segment entering and expressing within a cell can export its gene products as 'common goods' in neighboring cells and/or sieve elements, so that these common goods are redistributed among interconnected cells and complement the system.
evidence: This is stated as a model compatible with the observations.

claim: The demonstration that the protein M-Rep accumulates and functions in cells devoid of its encoding DNA-R is a proof of concept supporting the model of complementation across cells.
source: The demonstration that the protein M-Rep accumulates and functions in cells devoid of its encoding DNA-R is a proof of concept fully supporting this model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Plant mRNAs can move from cell to cell or long distance.
source: Numerous studies have shown that plant mRNAs (Kehr and Kragler, 2018) and proteins can move from cell to cell or long distance (Turnbull and Lopez-Cobollo, 2013; Lopez-Cobollo et al., 2016; Paultre et al., 2016), even from root to shoot.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Plant proteins can move from cell to cell or long distance, even from root to shoot.
source: Numerous studies have shown that plant mRNAs (Kehr and Kragler, 2018) and proteins can move from cell to cell or long distance (Turnbull and Lopez-Cobollo, 2013; Lopez-Cobollo et al., 2016; Paultre et al., 2016), even from root to shoot.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mechanisms and specific control of plant mRNAs and proteins mobility is vastly elusive.
source: Unfortunately, the mechanisms and specific control of these mRNAs and proteins mobility is vastly elusive.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Concomitant infection of individual cells by all genomic segments is not necessary for FBNSV.
source: Here we introduce an additional concept in virology, which is compatible with empirical observations and which partially alleviates the insurmountable cost in highly multipartite viral systems such as FBNSV (Iranzo and Manrubia, 2012): because concomitant infection of individual cells by all genomic segments is not necessary, the associated putative cost should be much smaller if not nil at the within-host level.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The associated putative cost of multipartitism should be much smaller if not nil at the within-host level for FBNSV.
source: Here we introduce an additional concept in virology, which is compatible with empirical observations and which partially alleviates the insurmountable cost in highly multipartite viral systems such as FBNSV (Iranzo and Manrubia, 2012): because concomitant infection of individual cells by all genomic segments is not necessary, the associated putative cost should be much smaller if not nil at the within-host level.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that co-infection is not necessary.

claim: The analogous cost upon between-host transmission and the mechanisms of its compensation remain to be understood.
source: We earlier discussed the fact that the analogous cost upon between-host transmission and the mechanisms of its compensation remain to be understood (Gallet et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A multicellular way of life could be adopted in other multicomponent genetic entities if functional complementation could occur at a supra-cellular level.
source: Such a multicellular way of life could be adopted in other multicomponent genetic entities, such as other multipartite viruses, segmented viruses which often fail to encapsidate all genome segments together (Luque et al., 2009; Wichgers Schreur and Kortekaas, 2016; Brooke, 2017), satellites, and defective interfering particles, if functional complementation could occur at a supra-cellular level.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about broader implications, supported by citations.

claim: Segmented viruses often fail to encapsidate all genome segments together.
source: Such a multicellular way of life could be adopted in other multicomponent genetic entities, such as other multipartite viruses, segmented viruses which often fail to encapsidate all genome segments together (Luque et al., 2009; Wichgers Schreur and Kortekaas, 2016; Brooke, 2017), satellites, and defective interfering particles, if functional complementation could occur at a supra-cellular level.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The inoculation of plants with the FBNSV infectious clone routinely yields a productive viral infection.
source: As shown in all the publications cited in this paragraph, the inoculation of plants with this infectious clone routinely yields a productive viral infection, meaning that the FBNSV particles can be purified from these infected plants and very efficiently transmitted to new healthy ones by aphids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: FBNSV particles can be purified from infected plants and very efficiently transmitted to new healthy ones by aphids.
source: As shown in all the publications cited in this paragraph, the inoculation of plants with this infectious clone routinely yields a productive viral infection, meaning that the FBNSV particles can be purified from these infected plants and very efficiently transmitted to new healthy ones by aphids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Nanoviruses replicate and accumulate primarily in phloem vascular bundles of the upper part of the plant, in companion cells and phloem parenchyma cells of the stem, petioles and main leaf veins.
source: Nanoviruses, and thus FBNSV, replicate and accumulate primarily in phloem vascular bundles of the upper part of the plant, in companion cells and phloem parenchyma cells of the stem, petioles and main leaf veins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nanoviruses.

claim: The FBNSV genome is composed of eight circular ssDNA segments of around 1 kb each.
source: The FBNSV genome is composed of eight circular ssDNA segments of around 1 kb each (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a description of FBNSV and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Infection by FBNSV distorts the anatomy of the phloem tissues.
source: Infection by FBNSV distorts the anatomy of the phloem tissues and so distinguishing between phloem parenchyma cells, companion cells and sieve elements is difficult and sometimes impossible in our petiole cross-sections.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental work.

claim: ssDNA viruses replicate and accumulate in the nucleus of their host cells.
source: For this reason, and because we were primarily interested by cells where the viral DNA replicates (ssDNA viruses replicate and accumulate in the nucleus of their host cells), we quantified the fluorescence only in those cells where a nucleus was clearly revealed by the DAPI staining, so in cells other than the sieve tubes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ssDNA viruses.

claim: Different resolution settings do not differentially affect green and red fluorescence in the quantification approach used.
source: We wished to confirm that different resolution settings do not differentially affect green and red fluorescence.
evidence: This is stated as a concern that was experimentally addressed.

claim: The stability of red and green probes was similar and a possible differential degradation could not bias the localization and correlation/regression analysis.
source: Another potential concern was the time spanning between microscopy slide preparation and the end of the observation/quantification. Due to the experimental design, it was important to confirm that the stability of red and green probes was similar and that a possible differential degradation could not bias our localization and correlation/regression analysis.
evidence: This is stated as a concern that was experimentally addressed.

claim: The regression analysis from two sets of images acquired at different times and resolutions gave remarkably similar results.
source: We first quantified the fluorescence of R1-Green and R2-Red probes in petiole N°43 with fast acquired images (resolution 512 × 512). We then repeated the observation 2 weeks later on the same microscopy slides with a resolution 1024 × 1024. The cells quantified at the two dates were not necessarily the same as we could not be sure to retrieve all of them. The regression analysis from these two sets of images gave remarkably similar results, demonstrating that the resolution setting and the aging of the preparation could only have negligible effect (if at all) on our conclusions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different acquisition conditions.

claim: The resolution setting and the aging of the preparation could only have negligible effect (if at all) on the conclusions.
source: The regression analysis from these two sets of images gave remarkably similar results, demonstrating that the resolution setting and the aging of the preparation could only have negligible effect (if at all) on our conclusions.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar results obtained under different conditions.

claim: The total viral load varies between distinct petioles because of a 'natural' variance across infected plants and because some were harvested at different dpi.
source: We did not analyze the fluorescence quantification data set as a whole (pooling cells from distinct petioles) because the virus-associated fluorescence intensity is not directly comparable. The total viral load varies in between distinct petioles because of a 'natural' variance across infected plants and because some were harvested at different dpi.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for the statistical approach used.

claim: The auto-fluorescence of the infected tissues varied across petioles because of the time of infection, the total viral load and presumably other unknown factors.
source: The auto-fluorescence of the infected tissues also varied across petioles because of the time of infection, the total viral load and presumably other unknown factors.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental work.

claim: The timing of infection did not significantly increase the frequency of co-occurrence of segments within individual cells.
source: We here use the available data to show that, in our experimental conditions, the timing of infection did not significantly increase the frequency of co-occurrence of segments within individual cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phloem is the only tissue infected by nanoviruses.
source: B-I show cross sections of infected faba bean petioles, with phloem (ph, the only tissue infected by nanoviruses), and xylem (xy) bundles indicated in B.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nanoviruses.
